decisions.quote: Recently, we found hypomethylation of OXT in patients with Major Depressive Disorder (MDD) compared to healthy controls (HC). Since the replicability of findings is a key point of criticism in (epi‑)genetic research, we aimed to confirm our previous findings in a pre-registered study (data was stored in a database prior to pre-registration) within a new sample of n = 85 patients with MDD and n = 85 HC.
decisions.reason: No prior adjudication or state file exists for this work. The supplied primary source is abstract-only and explicitly states that the authors retested and confirmed their previous finding of OXT hypomethylation in patients with Major Depressive Disorder compared to healthy controls in a new sample (n = 85 MDD, n = 85 HC). However, the abstract refers to the original only as 'our previous study' / 'our previous findings' without an in-text citation or reference list. While shipped row 821 (Sanwald et al., 2020, 10.1016/j.jad.2020.07.068, 'Relation of promoter methylation of the structural oxytocin gene to critical life events in major depression: A case control study') is a plausible match by the same research group, the unresolved question is which specific citation(s) in the full text identify 'our previous study' and whether shipped row 821 is the sole replicated report rather than another related earlier Sanwald et al. paper.

decisions.quote: This study sought to directly replicate a previous investigation that demonstrated a positive association between altruism and indices of mating success (Arnocky et al., 2017). Participants (n = 445; 329 women, 116 men; Mage = 22.9 years) completed measures of altruism, personality, self-reported mating success, lifetime sexual partners, lifetime casual sex partners, and frequency of copulation with their current sexual partner.
decisions.reason: No prior adjudication or state file exists for this work. The replication title ('Altruism does not predict mating success in humans: A direct replication.') and abstract explicitly retest the positive association between altruism and mating success reported by Arnocky et al. (2017). Shipped row 1003 (Arnocky, Piché, Albert, Ouellette, & Barclay, DOI 10.1111/bjop.12208, 'Altruism predicts mating success in humans') is the exact same original study: Crossref metadata confirms it was published online in July 2016 (hence year_o = 2016 in the shipped row) and in print in British Journal of Psychology Vol. 108, Issue 2, pp. 416-435 in 2017 (hence 'Arnocky et al., 2017' in the abstract). Target 0 is therefore already represented by input_row_index 1003.

decisions.quote: Three-level, linear growth models (time-student-school) were used to estimate treatment effects, found for print awareness, elision, rhyming, and the screener (print and letter knowledge, phonological awareness), replicating previous findings for the screener, rhyming, and print knowledge, and extending them to elision.
decisions.reason: No prior adjudication or state file exists for this work. The supplied primary text contains only the publisher abstract, acknowledgments, and funding note, with no in-text citations or reference list. The abstract states that the randomized trial replicated previous findings for the screener, rhyming, and print knowledge, and the acknowledgments state that the article 'extends findings from data provided in previously published reports.' Although shipped row 8 (Bailet, Repper, Piasta, & Murphy, 2009, 10.1177/0022219409335218, 'Emergent Literacy Intervention for Prekindergarteners at Risk for Reading Failure') is an earlier intervention report from the same program, the unresolved question is which specific published report(s) are cited in the full text as the source of the replicated screener, rhyming, and print knowledge findings, and whether input_row_index 8 is the sole replicated target or whether additional prior reports are also retested.

corrected_value.title: When worry about climate change leads to climate action: How values, worry and personal responsibility relate to various climate actions

decisions.quote: The current study replicates and extends recent work (Bouman et al., 2020; Syropoulos & Markowitz, 2022) which found a meaningful and robust relationship between people's feelings of responsibility to reduce climate change, their worry about climate change, and their belief that climate change is caused by humans. Importantly, these findings were consistently observed across 31 different European countries, and when controlling for crucial socio-demographic variables.
decisions.reason: No prior adjudication or state file exists for this work. Both the Introduction (line 73) and the Discussion (line 101) explicitly identify Bouman et al. (2020) alongside Syropoulos & Markowitz (2022) as the recent European cross-national work whose empirical finding—that personal responsibility to reduce climate change predicts greater worry about climate change and belief in human-caused climate change—is directly replicated using Wave 10 European Social Survey data across 31 countries. The source reference list (lines 224-230) verifies the identity of Bouman et al. (2020) ('When worry about climate change leads to climate action: How values, worry and personal responsibility relate to various climate actions', Global Environmental Change, 2020). The sole shipped row (input_row_index 1549, Syropoulos & Markowitz, 2022, 10.1016/j.jenvp.2022.101868) matches sibling target_index 0 and is a distinct paper by different authors in a different journal; report equivalence does not apply.

corrected_value.authors: Tucker MA, Taylor K, Merchant R, et al.
corrected_value.title: Scopolamine does not impact declarative and motor memory consolidation across a night of sleep or a day of wakefulness.

decisions.reason: No prior adjudication or state file exists for this work. As a second empirical aim stated in the Abstract (line 137), Introduction (lines 247-257), Results (lines 426-436, Table 1), and Discussion (lines 473-480), the authors retest their previously published finding from Tucker et al. (2018) [26] that intrinsic motivation (measured via the same four Intrinsic Motivation Inventory items) correlates positively with paired-associates acquisition and retention change across a 12-hour sleep/wake interval without differentially favoring sleep over wake. In Results and Discussion, they explicitly compare the new verbal paired-associates correlations against those of [26], replicating the positive association with training and retest recall and the lack of a sleep-vs-wake difference, but not the correlation with change from training to retest. Reference 26 (line 623) verifies the identity of Tucker et al. (2018) in Neurobiology of Learning and Memory (155: 371-378). This work is completely distinct from the sole shipped row (input_row_index 309, Ellenbogen et al., 2009) and from sibling target_index 0 (Ellenbogen et al., 2006).
